utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. If I could remind you, Ms. Cakar, that the affirmation that you made at the beginning of your evidence still applies. And now Mr. Dobbyn.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, just before I continue with questioning there is one quick matter I would like to bring up. Yesterday, a video was shown and it was admitted as P442. At that time, my learned colleague, Ms. Residovic, stated that the same video had already been marked for identification as P363 through the witness Peter Bouckaert. And at that time I stated that this was not the same video. And this is at page 5159 of the transcript. Having had the chance to review it, I stand corrected now and I thank my colleagues for bringing this to my attention. They are the same video, they appeared twice on our 65 ter exhibit list. And to avoid confusion, I would propose that with the Chamber's permission that P442 be removed from the exhibits and P363 which was marked for identification now be admitted as they are the same video and it would clear up the issue of having this other video just marked for identification and not admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as I already said yesterday, it is true the video recording itself and everything that was said by the witness is completely identical on both videos. However, the video footage that was shown yesterday, there is a time stamp or a notification about the time. I cannot really suggest to the Chamber, but it might be good for the previous one, from the Witness Bouckaert to be taken off the list. Because, after all, this video material has been shown to this witness and the time is identified on the video footage. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. At the moment, I would be prepared to leave both and let confusion reign.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: If that is the position the Chamber wishes to take, then certainly we don't have any issue with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Cakar, yesterday, and this is at page 5188 in the transcript, in response to a question you agreed that the shooting that could be heard in the video-clip was not actually recorded when you were at the location known as Brace's house. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember when it was recorded in the yard of the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm just not quite clear from your answer. Was the sound of the shooting that can be heard in the video, was that recorded while you were in the yard of the house or not?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The shooting sound is from the time when we were at the check-point before we actually arrived in the courtyard of the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And this was on the same date, the 12th of August, 2001?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Was Minister Boskoski at the same location at the check-point when this shooting was taking place?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And also yesterday at page 5190, you agreed with my learned colleague's proposition that Minister Boskoski had not been managing anything while he was present in the Ljuboten area. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there around two hours, so from 3.00 to 5.00 p.m. and during these couple of hours, while we were in the courtyard of the house, I did not notice for the Minister Boskoski to communicate with anybody or to have any formal conversation. I haven't noticed such a thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Were you at Minister Boskoski's side throughout those entire two hours?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were in the courtyard, in one part of the courtyard, together with the cameraman and few more people who were accompanying Minister Boskoski that particular day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And my question is: Were you right at his side for those two hours?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was there in the courtyard of the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Were you privy to all the conversations he had with anyone else during those two hours?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In general, I was there quite close to him, but during a portion of that time, I was moving around with the cameraman. But, in general, I was there, right close to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: My question is: Were you privy to all conversations he had and could you say precisely what he said during any of these conversations?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I already said, mainly throughout the time I was close to him, but I cannot precisely recall all the conversations, but I know that these were not formal conversations. I can recall this because of the fact since these conversations did not represent an information for me personally. From these conversations, I did not get any information about what was going on. If there were formal conversations, I would have received at least some kind of information about what was going on there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Why do you say would you have received some kind of information?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have certain knowledge. I would get some idea. If there were such conversations taking place, I would have had some knowledge about what was going on, but I didn't have any.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Are you saying it was Minister Boskoski's practice that if he gave directions or orders to his subordinates he would then pass those directions or orders on to the media?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this was the only occasion that I actually accompanied Minister Boskoski at such an event. I don't have the experience, I wouldn't know how Minister Boskoski would act in certain -- such situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: You stated that during a portion of the time you were moving around with the cameraman. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were sitting in the courtyard, in the upper right-hand corner, at a table made out of stone, and I remember right next to this table there was a small low stone wall, and we were sitting there with the cameraman when Minister Boskoski went to the wall, the cameraman went there to take the shot. I was standing right next to the cameraman. We completed the filming. We went back. We sat at the same table, and this is how we spent this hour, hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Who was it that told Minister Boskoski that terrorists had entered from Kosovo and that there was an action going on to arrest them?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, if I could make that more clear. I'm asking who told Minister Boskoski this.

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: So that was a conversation that you weren't privy to?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Before we entered the courtyard, this is the general information I received when we were sitting at the table, the minister was with several people around him, but I cannot remember what was this conversation. The only thing I remember is that I received this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: So if you don't remember this conversation, can you say for certain whether or not Minister Boskoski gave any directions or orders whether formally or informally during this time?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was there, in my presence, he did not issue such instructions. I was not a witness of such a situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that you don't know what was said outside of your presence?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, at page 5175 of yesterday's transcript, you agreed again with my learned colleague that Minister Boskoski was very open with journalists and you said that it was known he wanted to be present in the media. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And you've testified that throughout the crisis period in 2001, you were a parliamentary reporter. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: During this crisis period in 2001, as minister of the interior, did Ljube Boskoski often appear in the media and on the television?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, quite often.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And what would he be doing during these appearances on the television?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes he was giving a statement, sometimes they would register his presence at a particular location. He was filmed, registered in different kind of situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: When you say they would register his presence at different locations or at particular locations, what sort of locations are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Wherever he would go in his function, his position as a minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Would he ever be recorded appearing in other crisis areas?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I remember, I specifically recall one more material. This is not what I did, but this was when Minister Boskoski was touring several regions, and I remember that he was accompanied by a crew from the Macedonian Television, and I remember there was a news story made about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And do you recall what regions or what locations these were?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember specifically. I did not work on this material. However, I know it was made, and this was -- it was not that far away from the time when this event happened that we are discussing here today. It was right before or after these particular events.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: In these media appearances, would he comment on the security situation in Macedonia at that time?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was responding to the questions by the journalists or giving a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And in this appearance where he was touring the regions or any other appearances that you were aware of, was he also recorded in the presence of Ministry of Interior units or forces?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I cannot recall about such details.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Okay. You also testified that on the occasion when you were directed to -- to go the Ljuboten area, a car from the Ministry of Interior came to pick you up. How often would it happen that a car from the Ministry of Interior would be sent to pick up a reporter?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my situation, personally, this was the first time. As a journalist, I found myself in such situation for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Well, actually, my question doesn't just apply to you personally, but in general. How often were vehicles sent from the Ministry of Interior to pick up reporters?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer this question, because I was not at a position where I would have insight in these kind of issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Well, if I could perhaps refer you to paragraph 10 of your consolidated statement, and there you stated: "My chief told me, You and the cameraman have to go on duty. An official car from the ministry is coming to pick you up. I was very concerned about my safety. Normally we have our own cars but it was very clearly said to me, An official car is coming to pick you up. I'm not 100 per cent sure about the word ministry but whenever this phrase was used, it was clear to us that it is a car from the ministry." Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Then I also said that I was not sure whether when the task was assigned to me, whether the editor actually told me a car from the Ministry of Interior is going to come and pick us up. But if the editor would say so, then I could have assumed that the car comes from the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Well, from this part of your statement I've just read, doesn't that show that -- that it did happen on other occasions, that cars from the ministry would come to pick up reporters? Or is my understanding of that incorrect?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assumed that it was a car from the Ministry of the Interior, because it looked most logical to me at that moment. This was a ministry that was dealing with the security issues, and Minister Boskoski was the exposed figure at this particular period.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Are you aware of vehicles from the Ministry of the Interior picking up any reporters, any other reporters --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness, at least three times responded to the same question, and I believe that this kind of questions are no longer fair for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Residovic. Carry on, Mr. Dobbyn.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Are you aware of any other occasions where any other reporters had been picked by vehicles from the Ministry of the Interior and taken to crisis areas?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said. I found myself in such situation for the first time. I did not hold the position where I would have insight in the general developments. From my position, I only had insight in what was going on with me and my personal tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I will move on then. Could you perhaps tell us in general terms what sort of image did Minister Boskoski have in the media?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Image of a minister who would like to see himself in the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: In your statement, and it was raised again on cross-examination yesterday, you said it was your impression that the minister wanted to be recorded as a hero. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Was it your impression that he perhaps tried to cultivate this image himself through other appearances?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Simply this was his style, at least this is how I interpreted these kind of issues. I didn't see these as a will to improve something, just as a style of fulfilling his function.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: In your view, do you believe he had the image of someone who was an involved leader, someone who was a hands-on sort leader or was he more of a type of minister who would stay in the background?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand this question well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Well, from his appearances in the media, in your view was his image of someone when a security situation arose would perhaps go out in the field or was he more likely to remain back in his office and deal with the situation from there?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I haven't analysed him to this extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Okay. Moving on, at page 5188 of yesterday's transcript, you agreed with my learned colleague that your report was arranged or massaged to make it appear more dramatic. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: In 2001, during the year of the security crisis, were there many such broadcasts that were massaged to show Minister Boskoski in a more dramatic light?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot really tell, because I was not involved much in this part of the work.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: So, to your knowledge, the only report that was massaged or shown in such a way was this particular report shot in -- about the incident in Ljuboten. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Well, perhaps you could clarify your answer for me, please. What did you mean?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already mentioned yesterday, there was a tendency of stronger emphasis placed on certain issues. However, I was not a journalist who would be involved in the monitoring of these events on a daily basis, and that is why I cannot confirm this conclusion of yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Okay. Well, what was the purpose of this tendency to place a stronger emphasis on certain issues. What was the purpose of that?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guess, at that moment, I don't know. Probably it was an editorial policy issue maybe to raise the level of optimism or maybe to improve the trust in the security forces, I don't know. This is how I would understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Just one moment, Your Honours, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Do you think this was also done to improve the trust in the leaders of the security forces?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not have that impression at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: In your consolidated statement, you refer to a close relationship between your editor and Minister Boskoski. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this question was not being asked, was not asked in the cross-examination and my colleague did not elaborate that directly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No, but I believe the subject has been adequately raised by the tenor of much of the cross-examination. Yes, Mr. Dobbyn.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I will repeat that question for you, Ms. Cakar. Do you recall in your consolidated statement referring to what appeared to be a close relationship between your editor and Minister Boskoski. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that could have -- they knew each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And you testified that the way your report ended up being presented was as a result of decisions made by your editor. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And what do you think his reason for doing this was?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I object to this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness cannot know what the intention of her editor was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: She has expressed a general opinion as to the purpose of certain adjustments to the tone of broadcasts published. Mr. Dobbyn, carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Do you think that this adjustment to the video that your editor suggested, did this have the effect of -- in this video, perhaps, showing the leadership skills of Minister Boskoski in a better light?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment I did not try to penetrate his motivation. I did not think about his motivation at all, because simply, I just did not want to take that task willingly. I did not want to create and massage this material in the way that was suggested.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I understand and I appreciate that this was not something that you wished to do. But in your view, what was the overall effect of the difference between the report you wanted to give and the report your editor made you give?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the recorded material, those shots that were made when the Minister Boskoski was standing next to that fence, at that moment there was -- there was no shooting, and initially that's what the material looked like. Only when the clips from the check-point were shown, only then we could have heard shooting which only -- which were only strong during that short time interval and this is all that we had. And this was inserted to accompany the picture when the audio part was recorded. I insisted that this remain like this and in the text to hear that the Minister Boskoski was only there in the afternoon, in the immediate vicinity of the Ljuboten village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Didn't your editor also insist on a clip of the minister being present in the video that was shown?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not understand you well. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Well, in paragraph 29 of your consolidated statement, you said that your editor Dimovski commented: "Where is the minister here? I told him that we do have a part of the video showing the minister observing the situation. He told me to put this scene in." Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. However, he expected that there would be more footage, and we only had that clip, only those few shots.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And in paragraph 30 of your consolidated statement, you stated: "In my version of the text for the comment I was planning to comment, the minister of the interior was observing the operation of the security forces. Also, this comment, the editor didn't like. He insisted that I say that the minister directed the operation." Do you recall this?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. The editor insisted on using a stronger phrasing, a formulation in which the role of the Minister Boskoski will be more prominent while I insisted on a formulation that would only show that he was only there in the immediate vicinity in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And did your editor tell you why he wanted the role of Minister Boskoski to be more prominent?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was no explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, yesterday, and again this is at page 5149 of the transcript you agreed with my learned colleague that your report, as relied upon by Human Rights Watch actually contained false information and that you disagreed with this approach. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to express myself more precisely I would say that in the first part, wherein the report which pertains to the Minister Ljube Boskoski, that talks about him, it does not correspond to what the Macedonian Television team observed in the course of the hour and a half that was in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: How many other news reports with false information were you involved in making?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never in a situation like that before.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: So throughout your reports that you were involved in throughout the crisis period in 2001, this was the only report that you feel contained false information?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we would like to ask our colleague to list the page in which the witness said that she used false information, because we cannot -- that she used false information because I cannot identify it in the transcript. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Dobbyn, can you?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, starting at page 5193 and continuing into 5194 there were questions about the presence of Minister Boskoski and the length of time he was present and particularly, the information in the report that he was present throughout the entire operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mm-hm. Continue, Mr. Dobbyn.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: So I'll repeat my earlier question which was: In the reports that you prepared throughout the crisis period in 2001, are you saying that this was the only report that you were involved in, in which false information was put across?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the only case in which the influence of the editor-in-chief was so important because on that day he was present there. There have been other situations and events where he was not directly present, although it would have happened quite often that he was present at the desk where the news were produced. However, in this situation, he was present there and, in that manner, he was able to directly influence the contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And this is the only report of yours in which that was done?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wanted to have insight, understanding and influence about almost everything that came out of the journalist's text. This was not an unusual practice. However, he was not always in a position to be able to do that. And, as I said, it was not unusual that he shows interest and that he tries to influence the texts that journalists wrote. And not only those that dealt with anything that came from the crisis regions, but about everything else that was presented in the Macedonian Television news.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I am actually asking something a little more specific than that, and I would ask to you please listen to the question and just answer my question. And my question is: Was this report about the events in Ljuboten the only report that you were involved in which contained false information?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know what? When a journalist produces a report --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I'm sorry to cut you off --

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must answer -- I apologise as well. Because I cannot generally accept the formulation "false information."

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Really, this is a -- a question which really only calls for a yes or no answer. And my question to you is this the only report of yours that ever contained information which turned out to be incorrect, not true? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Cakar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And I have no further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Cakar. You will pleased to know that concludes the questions to be asked. The Chamber would thank you for your attendance in The Hague and the assistance you have given. And the court officer will now show you out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time the Prosecution would call Mr. Howard Tucker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: While that is being arranged, could the Chamber draw the attention of all counsel to two matters which will affect the programme next week. First, on the Wednesday of next week, there has been called a Plenary of Judges, which will commence at 12.00, and it is not clear precisely when it will finish. Out of caution, the Chamber believes it should sit at 3.30 rather than 2.15 on the Wednesday, and that will allow us two complete hour-and-a-half sessions until 7.00. The second issue affects Thursday. On that day, the Chamber has to deliver judgement in another matter. The nature of that other matter and the size demands that we use one of the larger courtrooms, and it is therefore necessary to fit in with another Trial Chamber and the Appeal Chamber which is also delivering a decision on that day in the same courtroom. As a consequence, the Chamber is not able to commence the delivery of its judgement until mid-afternoon. It appears to the Chamber in the circumstances that it is really impractical to think of sitting in this trial on the Thursday. We would have perhaps three quarters of an hour before and perhaps three quarters of an hour after, which is really not of great use and is very disruptive to the evidence of whoever happens to be the witness and whichever counsel happens to be dealing with the witness. So we believe, regrettably, that for the reasons indicated, it will be necessary not to sit on Thursday of next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could I ask you to please read aloud the affirmation on the card that has been given to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If you could sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And Mr. Saxon has questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Is your name Howard Tucker?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And are you an investigator working for the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: Yes. Currently I'm the head of office at the field offices in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And when did you begin your work with the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: I came on secondment initially in April of 1998, and then returned as an investigator in the following year in May of 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Tucker, do you recall signing a witness statement for the Office of the Prosecutor on the 25th of March, 2006?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly ask the witness to come closer to the microphones. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Tucker, the interpreters have asked if you can move up a bit closer, sit a bit closer to the microphone so they can hear you clearer. Thank you. And I should remind you and myself that because we're speaking in the same language, both you and I need to try to pause between sentences so that the interpreters can catch up with what we're saying.

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: Yes, I understand sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The other word of advice, Mr. Tucker, would be try to speak to Mr. Saxon or to the Bench which will encourage your voice to be a little bit louder.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Tucker, do you recall on that same day, the 25th of March, 2006, that your statement was certified by an officer of the registry of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: I do, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And that was done -- and again, Mr. Tucker, remember to -- let's pause for a moment between my question and your answer so that we don't strain the goodwill of the interpreters. And that certification was done pursuant to 92 bis. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: I do, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And on that occasion, did you have an opportunity to review your statement in your native English language?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: I did, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And are the contents of your statement true and correct to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: They are, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time I would seek to tender the statement of Mr. Tucker under Rule 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P443, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, in summation, as you have already heard, Mr. Tucker is a investigator currently working for the Office of the Prosecutor. In early 2002, Mr. Tucker was tasked with monitoring the exhumation project that was scheduled to take place at the Muslim cemetery in the village of Ljuboten. Mr. Tucker took part in meetings with representatives of the government of Macedonia, and other representatives of the international community regarding preparations for the exhumation that occurred in Ljuboten. When the exhumation began at Ljuboten on the 7th of April, 2002, Mr. Tucker was present and carried out such tasks as the recording of his own observations during the exhumation, liaison work with a NATO Explosive Ordinance Disposal team that was also present, liaising with relatives of the deceased and with judicial authorities and securing evidence found at the graves with ICTY evidence security tape. Mr. Tucker was also present at the Macedonian Forensic Institute while autopsies were performed on the exhumed bodies. During the autopsies, Mr. Tucker took possession of and recorded any ballistic material that was found in, around, or on the body or in the clothing of the deceased.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Tucker, in your statement, you describe in detail how the exhumations of deceased persons at the Muslim cemetery of Ljuboten were carried out in April 2002, and you also describe the autopsies that were performed after the exhumations at the Macedonian Forensic Institute in Skopje. My first question for you is this: Prior to the start of the exhumations in early April 2002, did any meetings take place to discuss plans to carry out the exhumations?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, there were many meetings starting from November 2001, right up until the day prior to the exhumation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And did you participate -- let me step back for a minute. When you say "many meetings starting from November 2001," were those meetings in November 2001 focused on the Ljuboten exhumation or the exhumations of other sites of potential crimes in Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: Other sites of potential exhumations in Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. When did you begin -- when did meetings, planning meetings for the exhumation at Ljuboten begin, approximately?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: In the early part of 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you participate in these meetings?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Who else participated in these meetings with you?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: The various authorities of Macedonia. The international community, and NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Let's go a little bit more slowly. When you say, "the various authorities of Macedonia," could you be a bit more specific please. Which authorities or which institutions are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: The Macedonian Ministry of Justice, the Skopje Forensic Institute, and the Ministry of Interior police.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And when you refer to the international community, can you be a bit more specific? Representatives of which institutions or organisations were at those meetings?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: The organisations of OSCE, EUMM and NATO represented by task force Fox, as it was referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Tucker, what was your role in these meetings?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: My main function was that of a monitor. However, at the meetings, I played the role of coordinator between all the various agencies that were involved in the exhumation project.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And at times did you make suggestions or recommendations at these meetings?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And were your suggestions accepted or not?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: Yes. They were -- they were accepted and some weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So if I can understand your response, some of your suggestions were accepted, but some were not?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Tucker, why were these meetings necessary before the exhumation -- let me step back. Were these meetings necessary before the exhumation in Ljuboten could take place?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: Yes, they were, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And why -- why was that?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: The situation in Macedonia at that particular time was quite tense. And in order for the exhumation project to be successful there had to be a great deal of issues covered and decided upon before the exhumation could proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you give a few examples of some of these issues that needed to be discussed and worked out.

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: I suppose the first one would be the general security conditions in relation to the Macedonian authorities who were going to be present and conducting the exhumation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mm-hm?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: It was necessary to liaise with the family of the victims because there was a lot of distrust from their perspective in relation to anything to do with the Macedonian authorities. Similarly, from the Macedonian authorities side, there was a great deal of concern about the -- about the security of the party who would attend there. Agreement had to be conducted or discussions with NATO, OSCE, and the EUMM on how they could contribute to the security situation generally and to assist the process of the exhumation going forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And in addition to that, would it be fair to say that there were other matters that also had to be discussed and agreed upon?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: Absolutely. The -- the actual practicalities of the process of the exhumation on what roles were to be taking place and the order of the exhumations, the integrity of the scene, the scene being the Muslim cemetery, the integrity of the remains of the victims and any artifacts that were found during exhumation and the general process for the autopsies and the similar concerns about the integrity of the remains and any artifacts found.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Tucker, at any time during these discussions, during the planning meetings was there ever - and I'm talking about these meetings that began in the first part of 2002 - was there ever a suggestion that the ICTY or the international community, or both, had taken control of the Ljuboten investigation?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: No, sir. That was never -- as far as I was concerned an issue. It was always going to be an exhumation conducted by the authorities of Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And during these planning meetings --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise. This is not an objection, but simply to indicate perhaps for the sake of the record and for Mr. Saxon that the witness at page 25, line 12 has answered or the question of my colleague, I apologise was "has," rather than "will" take control, I think this was the question of Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm grateful. That was my -- that was my question. Past tense, had taken, rather than will take. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Tucker, during these planning meetings, were any agreements made about certain tasks that you would perform during the exhumation process?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: Yes, sir. There were various functions that developed during the courses of the meetings that I would end up being responsible for.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And can you describe, then, the tasks that you performed when the exhumations began?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: I mentioned earlier one of the primary functions was the security coordination for the exhumation and that included the safety and security of all parties present. That involved liaising closely with the NATO forces and the Exploded Ordinance Disposal Unit. The other functions that I adopted was that of, I suppose I would call it in my own field from home, a scenes of crime officer and be responsible for certain aspects of the integrity of items and artifacts that were recovered and found.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: I was a family liaison officer, if you like, with the relatives of the victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: And a coordinating liaison officer between the exhumation team and OSCE and EUMM.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: At this time, Mr. Tucker, I have some documents that I would like to show you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I believe we have some binders with some materials to provide to you and to the Defence and we should have a copy for Mr. Tucker as well. And can I ask, please, if a copy of Mr. Tucker's statement could please be provided to him because there are some very specific details that the witness may need to refresh his memory upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Tucker, in your statement you describe how exhumations were performed two bodies at a time and at the scene each body was given a number as it was removed from the cemetery and placed in a body-bag. Can you please turn to what is tab 1 in your binder, please. This is Rule 65 ter number 71. The English ERN begins N000-4283 and Macedonian ERN N000-4206. Just preliminarily, Mr. Tucker, were you also present when autopsies were performed in the Forensic Institute of Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: Yes, I was, Your Honours, for each of the exhumations and autopsies that took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And you'll see in front of you in tab 1 it's a document dated the 9th of April, 2002. It's called section protocol. And this is a report describing an autopsy that was done on a body known as number 1. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: I do, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And at the end -- the last page we see that it is signed by Dr. Aleksej Duma and Dr. Zdravko Cakar and Zlatko Jakovski. And do you recall that these were the doctors who were performing all -- some or all of the autopsies?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: Some of the autopsies, yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. And can you recall from your memory the actual identity of body number 1, which person that was?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: I can't from memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Would it help to you refresh your memory if you take a look at the page in your statement where you discuss that?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: It would, Your Honours, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Could you please take a look at page 4 of your report -- of your statement, please. And are you able to see towards the bottom of the page the name of the person who was given ID number 1?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: I can, yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And who was that?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: That was Rami Jusufi.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Just so the -- Rami Jusufi, right?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: Rami Jusufi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Perhaps if that facilitates things for Mr. Saxon, we won't take any issue with the naming of each and every body and the names that have been associated by Mr. Tucker in the statement. If that facilitates the questioning by Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well. Then I'll simply note for the record that in the 92 bis written witness statement that has now been admitted into evidence, beginning on page 4, the names and identity number of each body that was exhumed at the village of Ljuboten can be found, and these numbers, then, will be corresponding to these autopsy protocols that we're now showing the witness. At this time, Your Honour, I would seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I believe it is 1D78, Your Honour. We believe it is already in evidence through Dr. Jakovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well. I was not aware of that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Tucker, I'm not going to show you the autopsy report on body number 2 because that autopsy report is also already admitted into evidence. But if you could -- before we leave this particular deceased, can you turn to tab 2, please.

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In tab 2 is also Exhibit 1D77. And were you present when the clothing of the deceased was examined?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well. And if we can turn now to what is tab 3, please. This is 65 ter number 63, and this is another section protocol, you'll see, Mr. Tucker, it is dated the 12th of April, 2002. This document is signed, if you go to the last page, by Drs. Duma, Boskovski and Stankov. And was this another autopsy were you were present after the exhumation of this particular body?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And what role, if any, did you have to play vis-a-vis ballistic material or materials that were found in or around or on a body at the autopsy?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: It was my responsibility to take these artifacts from the pathologists finding them, to record them and secure them in evidence -- for evidence, I should say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And could you turn now -- excuse me, before you turn the page --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P444, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you turn now to what is tab 4, we see this is a clothing, and I should say, for the record, tab 4 is 65 ter number 66. The English version begins with N000-4295. This is the -- you'll see this is a document dated 30 May 2002, Mr. Tucker, do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: I do, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And this particular document is signed by -- it says it is a clothing examination of the body known as number 3, and you see at the end that this examination was done by Dr. Popovska and it is also signed by Dr. Aleksej Duma.

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: From an investigative point of view, what was the purpose of these examinations of clothing?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: There are several factors related to the examination of the clothing. Initially to obtain details for potential identification purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What else?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: Then to examine the clothing for any signs of any damage that maybe correspond to any injuries found on the remains of the deceased. And also to examine the clothing for any -- any ballistic or other type of foreign material that may have some evidentiary value.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, would seek to tender the document that is at tab 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P445, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if we take a look, please, Mr. Tucker, at tab 5, this is 65 ter number 62, the English ERN begins with N000-4299. And you'll see this document is dated the 13th of April, 2002. It is another section protocol. It is the autopsy of body number 4, which, according to Mr. Tucker's statement at page 6 would be Kadri Jashari. And if you look at the last page, Mr. Tucker, you'll see that this section protocol says that the autopsy was performed by Drs. Cakar and Stankov and this protocol was also signed by Dr. Aleksej Duma. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: I do, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Tucker, what was the position of Dr. Duma at the time?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: Professor Duma was the director of the Forensic Institute and therefore the head of the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And was Dr. Duma one of the gentlemen or persons who participated in the planning meetings for the exhumations at Ljuboten?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: Yes, sir, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would seek to tender the document at tab 5, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P446, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you can turn now, please, to tab 6, Mr. Tucker, this is 65 ter number 68. The ERN, English version, begins with N000-4310 -- excuse me, 4303. Mr. Tucker, this is a -- this is the section protocol for body number 5, which according to page 9 of your statement is -- was the body identified as Xhelal Bajrami. And it is dated 15th of April, 2002. And we see at the end the autopsy was performed by Drs. Boskovski and Davceva and the report was also signed by Dr. Duma. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: I do, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P447, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Tucker, if you can turn, please, to what is tab 7 in your binder. This is 65 ter number 77. The English ERN begins N000-4310. This is a document dated the 15th of April, 2002 from the medical faculty, Forensic Institute and Criminology from the University Kiril and Metodij. And this is a report of the clothing examination of body number 5, Mr. Xhelal Bajrami. And, again, if you go to the last page, Mr. Tucker, you'll see that the examination of the clothing was performed by Drs. Boskovski and Davceva and then the report was also signed by the director, Professor Duma. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: I do, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask that this document be tendered, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P448, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you could turn, Mr. Tucker, to what is tab 8 in your binder. And this is 65 ter number 73. The ERN version begins -- the English version begins with ERN N000-4312.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Tucker, you will see there is another section protocol dated 16th of April, 2002. And it is an autopsy report for what is referred to as -- here as body number 6, which, at page 9 of your 92 bis statement we see that that person, that body was the body of Sulejman Bajrami. And if you go to the last page, Mr. Tucker, you'll see that there were actually three doctors who performed this autopsy, Drs. Gutevska, Janevska and Davceva and the report was also signed by Dr. Duma. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: I do, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would seek to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P449, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you could turn, please, to what is tab 9 in the binder in front of you, Mr. Tucker. And this is 65 ter number 72. The ERN of the English version begins with N000-4316. Mr. Tucker, you will see that this is another report about an examination of clothing. It is dated the 16th of April, 2002. Again, the report is being sent to the Lower Court Skopje II, the investigating judge. And if you turn to the last page, Mr. Tucker, do you see that this examination of the clothing was performed by three doctors, Drs. Gutevska, Janevska and Davceva, and that the report was also signed by Professor Dr. Duma. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: I do, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask that this document be admitted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P450, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Tucker, if you could turn, please, to what is tab 10 in the binders in front of you. This is 65 ter number 74. The ERN of the English version starts at N000-4323. You'll this is another section protocol, Mr. Tucker, it's dated the 19th of April, 2002. And this autopsy report deals with body number 8. Body number 8 you identify in your written witness statement at page 12 as belonging to Muharem Ramadani. If you turn to the last page, Mr. Tucker, do you see that this autopsy report was signed by Drs. Cakar, Gutevska and Popovska and that the report was also signed by Professor Dr. Duma. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: I do, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time I would ask to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P451, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Finally, Mr. Tucker, I'd like to ask to you turn to what is tab 11 in the binder in front of you, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, this is 65 ter number 65. The English version begins with ERN N000-4327.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Tucker, if you take a look at the first page of the document you'll see that it is a clothing examination, dated the 19th of April, 2002, referring to the body number 8, whose autopsy report we saw a moment ago. And do you see at the last page, Mr. Tucker, that the examination of the clothing of Mr. Muharem Ramadani was performed by Drs. Cakar, Gutevska and Popovska, and the report was also signed by Dr. Duma. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: I do, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I would seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P452, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That would seem a very convenient moment, Mr. Saxon, for the first break, and we resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon. Oh, you have now concluded. Your last words.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: At this time my last words, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: At this time I believe the floor belongs to Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So encouraged, Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. I'm grateful to Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Tucker, my name is Guenael Mettraux and together with my colleague Edina Residovic, I'm appearing on of behalf Mr. Boskoski.

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And perhaps before we start, I would kindly ask that the court usher if he could give the documents back to Mr. Saxon which are now in front of Mr. Tucker.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Mr. Tucker, you've indicated to Mr. Saxon earlier on that in the course of the year 2001 and 2002, you had a number of meetings with the Macedonian authorities. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And you've also indicated to Mr. Saxon that in March and April of 2002 you had a number of meetings pertaining to the exhumation of Ljuboten. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: I do, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And you've indicated pursuant to a question of Mr. Saxon that there were also a number of meetings which you had with the Macedonian authority in relation to another exhumation or other exhumations and you indicated that such meeting took place in the year 2001. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And, Mr. Tucker, would those meetings relating to another exhumation, would they be the exhumation relating to crimes committed in the Neprosteno area. Is that the meetings you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: That's correct, they are, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And those meetings, Mr. Tucker, took place at the beginning of the month of November of 2001, the 9th, the 11th, the 13th, the 16th, the 18th, and the 24th of November of 2001. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: I don't remember the precise dates, but it was in November 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I'm grateful. Is that correct also Mr. Tucker that there were a number of other meetings later on in the month of November of 2001 which you attended on 27th, 28th, and 29th of November?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: Again, I can't remember specifically the dates, sir, I would need to have something to look at to be able to confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I will -- Mr. Tucker, I will show you the records of those meetings in a minute but would you agree that those meetings, the later meetings of the 27, 28, 29 had to do both to the Neprosteno investigation and the Ljuboten investigate of the OTP. Is that correct, sir,?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: I don't remember, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I will come to that in a minute. Is that correct, however, Mr. Tucker, that during those various meetings with the Macedonian authorities the Macedonian government undertook to provide you with the assistance needed for your own investigations. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: For our own -- I don't remember anything about conducting our own investigations, no, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, on the 27th of November of 2001, is that correct that the then minister of justice, an ethnic Albanian, at the time had stated to you that the Macedonian government had agreed to provide whatever assistance was required by you. Can you recall that?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: I can remember a meeting with a minister but I can't remember contents at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Can you recall that the minister of the time had undertaken to provide you with manpower and your other needs. Can you recall that?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: I don't remember that, no, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And can you recall, perhaps, that this meeting had to do, in part at least with the Ljuboten investigation. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: I don't recall the specifics, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: In that case I ask the registry perhaps to assist Mr. Tucker to show what is Rule 65 ter 1D611.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly ask the witness to speak closer to the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Mr. Tucker, I think you are being asked if you could move a little bit closer to the microphone. And, Your Honour, we also have binders both for the Court and the Prosecution, as well as for Mr. Tucker and which may assist the matter. The 65 ter number is 1D611 with an ERN 1D005526 and I can see that is already on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Mr. Tucker, this will be under tab 28 of your binder.

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, we believe there are no Macedonian version of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Mr. Tucker, I'll go through the document with you, if I may. If you look at the top of the document first, this is information taken in the form of an investigator's notes and under the title there is the purpose of the meeting and it says that it is a meeting arranged by Mr. Andrzej Szydlik, an operation officer of the ICTY for the visit of Mr. Dennis Milner, deputy chief of investigations. And the time and date are 27th of November of 2001, and the time is 12.30. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: I can, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And then you will see there's a location --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly ask the counsel and the witness to take a break between the questions and the answers so the interpreters can make it and translate everything. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Mr. Tucker, that was the second warning if we could pace ourselves between questions and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: There's an indication of a location which is the office of the Ministry of Justice in Skopje and there's a list of persons present. There is the Macedonian minister of justice whose name, I believe, is Ixet Memeti. Do you remember his name?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: I don't remember the gentleman's name. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And there is an assistant to the minister, Ms. Nedzana Mojseva [phoen]; Mr. Milner, the deputy chief of investigations; Mr. Szydlik; yourself, and an interpreter, Ms. Brajovic. If I can ask you to go down in this document, there is a paragraph starting with the word: "Mr. Dennis Milner." Can you see that? It is the first paragraph. It says this: "Mr. Dennis Milner introduced the representatives of the ICTY to those present. He stated for -- the reason for the visit was a follow-up to that of the Prosecutor." Perhaps I will interject a question at this stage. Do you recall that Ms. Del Ponte visited the Republic of Macedonia on the 20th and 21st of November, 2001, do you recall that event?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: I'm aware that Madam Prosecutor did visit Macedonia, but I don't recall the dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And if you go to the next paragraph, DM which is Mr. Dennis Milner, stated that it was his responsibility to assess the current situation in Macedonia relating to the investigations into the Nepostreno and Ljuboten. Can you see that.

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: I can, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And then it says: "He explained that the ICTY realised that there were more cases than this, but in respect of them, the dedicated investigation team had been appointed by the Prosecution to assess the available evidence." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: I can, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And if I may ask the registry to turn to the second page of that document. Perhaps I'll simply ask you at this stage to confirm that the notes were in fact taken by yourself. Is that correct, Mr. Tucker, if you look at the bottom of the document?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And if I ask to look at the first paragraph on the top of the page there are some comments attributed to the minister and that would the minister of justice mentioned on the previous page. But I'd like to turn to the second paragraph where the minister says the following: "He also stated that the authorities had agreed to provide whatever was required to conduct the investigations (manpower and other needs)." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Then there's another statement attributed to the minister, he then said: "He then spoke for a while about political issues involving the Nepostreno and Ljuboten investigations. He finished his speech by saying, I expect the ICTY to undertake specific actions about these two cases, Nepostreno and Ljuboten." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will simply ask that this document be MFI'd at this stage. We will seek later on to tender it; it will be used again.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D195 marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Is it correct, Mr. Tucker, that in the context of other meetings which you had with the Macedonian authorities, in particular the competent investigative organs of the state of Macedonia you were given the same assurances of assistance. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: That is correct, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And in particular on the same day that is the 27th of November of 2001, you met with then state prosecutor Mr. Stavre Dzikov. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: Can you repeat the date, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: The same day, Mr. Tucker, it would be the 27th of November, 2001.

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: I don't remember the date, but I assume there is an investigator's note that applies to that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: That's correct, and I will show it you in a second, sir. But can you recall or do you have a memory of the fact that during that meeting, Mr. Dzikov the state prosecutor offered full cooperation to the Office of the Prosecutor in relation to these investigations?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: I do. But I think there is an important distinction that I should make here at this stage, if Their Honours allow me. I think, and please correct me if I'm wrong, you're suggesting that the Macedonian authorities were going to supply the Office of the Prosecutor with resources for the Office of the Prosecutor to conduct investigations. I think that's basically what you were asking me, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, I should be more precise. At this stage, Mr. Tucker, I'm simply asking you whether the authorities are undertaken to assist you?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: It is actually the other way around.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, if we can turn to what is 65 ter 1D612. It has an ERN 1D005528. And this is again, Mr. Tucker, another one of those investigator's notes which was prepared at the time by yourself.

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm very sorry to interrupt. It's just if my colleague could please tell me what tab --

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I apologise. Thank you, Mr. Saxon. Your Honour, this is tab 29.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And perhaps going quickly through the header of this document, Mr. Tucker, you will see it is again an investigator's note the purpose is similar to the previous one. It was again arranged by your colleague Mr. Szydlik. The day is the same, the time is 1505, and those present include Mr. Dzikov, the public prosecutor of Macedonia, an assistant to Mr. Dzikov, Mr. Milner, Szydlik yourself and again your interpreter Ms. Brajovic. And if I can ask you to focus on the first full paragraph on this page I will read it for the record. "The public prosecutor welcomed the representatives from the ICTY. He stated that he was surprised to hear that the Prosecutor, ICTY, had only opened investigations into two cases, cases Nepostreno and Ljuboten. He felt there were many cases that required the interest and attention of the Tribunal. However, he assured those present of the full cooperation of his department during the investigation." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: I can, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, there again we would simply ask at this stage that this be MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D196, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And, Mr. Tucker, can you now remember that the next day that would be the 28th of November of 2001, a general agreement of cooperation was reached between you and the authorities competent to investigate the Ljuboten event in Macedonia. Do you have a memory of that?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: My memory is, is that the -- an agreement was made for the Macedonian authorities to investigate with us acting as monitors.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And the authorities with which you reached that agreements were the judicial authorities. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: I would be guessing. I can't remember who it was, who that final decision was made.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I can help you here. If you can turn to tab 31, Mr. Tucker, please. That would be Rule 65 ter 1D613 and it has an ERN of 1D00-5530. Again, no Macedonian. There again, Mr. Tucker, this is another one of those investigator's notes which were prepared by yourself as is evident from the last page if you wish to look at the last page. And it is dated the 28th of November of 2001, the meeting was again for the same purpose. It took place at this higher public prosecutor office in Skopje, and present were Mr. Serafimovski, the acting higher public prosecutor; Mr. Dragoljub you called him Mr. Sokic, I believe it is Mr. Cakic; Mr. Dragan Nikolovski, investigative judge; Mr. Nica, a criminal judge; Mr. Ljubomir Joleski, another criminal judge; Ms. Maja Konevska, deputy public prosecutor; Mr. Milner; Szydlik; yourself; and the interpreter, Ms. Brajovic. And if I can ask the registry to turn to the last page of that document. And again, Mr. Tucker, you can confirm that is a note that was prepared by you, by yourself?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: Yes, I can, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And the last sentence in this document or the last sentence in any case of your summary of this meeting reads that a general agreement of cooperation was established and promises of future close contact assured. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And is that correct to understand this sentence as suggesting that the agreement was reached by the people who were present during that meeting?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could MFI this document again, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D197, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Is it correct, Mr. Tucker, that this willingness or readiness of the authorities to assist you were given at all levels of the states, and by that I mean ministerial, judicial and forensic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: The agreement was not to assist us but to conduct the investigation and use us as a monitor, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I should go back to what is under tab 29 of your binder, which has now an MFI of 1D196. If I may ask the registry to turn to the second page of that document. And, Mr. Tucker, perhaps as a preliminary matter I'll ask you to confirm that to refer to Mr. Djikov I believe you used the letters "PP" for public prosecutor. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And if I may ask to you look at the fourth paragraph on the second page which starts with the words: "PP stated." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: I can, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And Mr. Dzikov says this: "Public prosecutor Mr. Dzikov stated that the willingness of the authorities to cooperate with the Tribunal is at all levels of the administration, including ministerial, judicial, forensic, crime scene technicians, (police) and the security force." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: I can, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And you would agree, I hope, that what the public prosecutor was stating there is that he and the Macedonian authorities were willing to assist you, or the Tribunal in any case. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: No, sir, I read it exactly as it says there, that the Macedonian authorities are willing to cooperate with the Tribunal, exactly as it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And this undertaking was to cooperate with yourself, the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: With the Office of the Prosecutor, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Is that correct also, Mr. Tucker, that your contacts with the Macedonian authorities date back, and when I mean your contacts I don't mean your personally, but the contacts of your office go back to the year 1999 and 2000 during and after the Kosovo crisis. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER.
utterances.text: I can't comment on that. My involvement with Macedonia was from the November of 2001, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
